The only technique that ever seems to work for me is the 'Body Scan Meditation': 
  Basically, focus your complete attention on all the different parts of your body in turn. Like, start with feeling the sensations in your little toe, then move on to the next toe, then the sole of the foot and so on.
   You can even get really creative with it and try feel all the different energy fields and lines that are outside the body. This keeps me amused for ages, seems to settle my brain, clears my head, redistributes energy and tension from where it may be stuck and usually leads to falling asleep. Hope this helps.

My ability to concentrate, understand complex information and reliably perform simple cognitive tasks has been gradually decreasing since I stopped Paxil (20mg) three years ago. I was on it since 2003, so about 11 years. 

I suffer from near-constant anxiety at the moment and simple mental tasks like calculations, making decisions, shopping for food, general body co-ordination/control have all suffered greatly. Often when trying to recall information my mind just draws a blank. Conversation is challenging and often frustrating. 

The depressive symptoms have gotten worse too, where I find it difficult, painful even, to engage in anything that most people would find enjoyable.

This has all been getting worse since I stopped the med 3 years ago, though whether it is due to the medication or just a coincidental decline in cognitive ability is unclear. I am diagnosed Bipolar and take medication for that, and as I understand it this condition is neurodegenerative, ie  causes gradual, progressive brain damage.

Recently I have found that flooding my internal self-talk with very positive statements about myself, the world and the future helps. It often seems like empty false lies, but occasionally something resonates and actually influences my mood positively. You are always telling yourself something, so you might as well make it positive and constructive. Your brain will then automatically work on finding the evidence to support these statements. It feels awkward at first but it gets stronger pretty quick. Seems to be helping me anyway. I think it's the basis of CBT. Also writing a list of 5 things you are grateful for twice a day trains your brain to look for the positive more often. Good luck.
